newsitem.title: FRANCE: Trade concerned over French malting barley exports.
newsitem.headline: Trade concerned over French malting barley exports.

text.p: France should produce more than enough malting barley this year to meet domestic demand and exporters are looking for third-country buyers to replace fading demand from EU neighbours faced with ample supplies, grain trade and industry sources said on Tuesday
"There will have enough malting barley to comfortably cover the needs of the French malting industry but where are we going to ship the excess barley?" one trader said.
Last year France exported some 500,000 tonnes of malting barley to Germany but a higher than expected crop is expected to curb German imports this year.
Belgium also bought French barley last year but is now expected to favour Germany and Denmark as suppliers.
French exporters said they were anxiously awaiting third-country buying to resume in the autumn as a rich EU malting barley crop was depressing spring barley prices.
Potential clients include China, eastern and central Europe and Latin America but here France will have to compete against other suppliers in the EU, Australia and Canada, they said.
German brokers and analysts expect traders to lobby the EU to support sales to the world market by granting export subsidies.

France's 1996 barley crop is expected to rise by at least 900,000 tonnes to 8.6 million tonnes this year, latest farm ministry estimates show. But French crop analyst Strategie Grains says output could reach 9.4 million tonnes due to a sharp increase in winter barley area and good yields for spring and winter barley.

Farm and market sources said spring barley has come off the fields in good shape for malting but winter barley suffered from excess protein. They said protein levels ranged from 11.5 to 12 percent. Maltsters favour protein content below 11.5 percent.

"If we look at winter barley, it will not be an easy year. But the malting industry is likely to use less winter barley and more spring barley this year, so we do not anticipate a supply problem," a malting industry source said.

He said some 25 percent of the total barley crop may qualify for malting purposes. This would amount to 2.2 million tonnes, including 1.2 million tonnes of spring barley for a domestic consumption estimated at 1.5 million tonnes. --Dominique Vidalon, Paris newsroom +331 4221 5432
